==Problem==
How many triangles with positive area have all their vertices at points <imath>(i,j)</imath> in the coordinate plane, where <imath>i</imath> and <imath>j</imath> are integers between <imath>1</imath> and <imath>5</imath>, inclusive?

<imath>\textbf{(A)}\ 2128 \qquad\textbf{(B)}\ 2148 \qquad\textbf{(C)}\ 2160 \qquad\textbf{(D)}\ 2200 \qquad\textbf{(E)}\ 2300</imath>

==Solution 1==
We can solve this by finding all the combinations, then subtracting the ones that are on the same line. There are <imath>25</imath> points in all, from <imath>(1,1)</imath> to <imath>(5,5)</imath>, so <imath>\dbinom{25}3</imath> is <imath>\frac{25\cdot 24\cdot 23}{3\cdot 2 \cdot 1}</imath>, which simplifies to <imath>2300</imath>. Now we count the ones that are on the same line. We see that any three points chosen from <imath>(1,1)</imath> and <imath>(1,5)</imath> would be on the same line, so <imath>\dbinom53</imath> is <imath>10</imath>, and there are <imath>5</imath> rows, <imath>5</imath> columns, and <imath>2</imath> long diagonals, so that results in <imath>120</imath>. We can also count the ones with <imath>4</imath> on a diagonal. That is <imath>\dbinom43</imath>, which is 4, and there are <imath>4</imath> of those diagonals, so that results in <imath>16</imath>. We can count the ones with only <imath>3</imath> on a diagonal, and there are <imath>4</imath> diagonals like that, so that results in <imath>4</imath>. We can also count the ones with a slope of <imath>\frac12</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, <imath>-\frac12</imath>, or <imath>-2</imath>, with <imath>3</imath> points in each. Note that there are <imath>3</imath> such lines, for each slope, present in the grid. In total, this results in <imath>12</imath>. Finally, we subtract all the ones in a line from <imath>2300</imath>, so we have <imath>2300-120-16-4-12=\boxed{(\textbf{B})\ 2148}</imath>

==Solution 2==
There are <imath>5 \times 5 = 25</imath> total points in all. So, there are <imath>\dbinom{25}3 = 2300</imath> ways to choose the three vertices for the triangle. However, there are some cases where they 3 points chosen results in a straight line.

There are <imath>10 \times 10 = 100</imath> cases where the 3 points chosen make up a vertical or horizontal line.

There are <imath>2\left(1+\dbinom{4}3+\dbinom{5}3+\dbinom{4}3+1\right)=40</imath> cases where the 3 points all land on the diagonals of the square.

There are <imath>3 \times 4=12</imath> ways where the 3 points make the a slope of <imath>\frac{1}{2}</imath>, <imath>-\frac{1}{2}</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, and <imath>-2</imath>.

Hence, there are <imath>100+40+12=152</imath> cases where the chosen 3 points make a line. The answer would be <imath>2300-152=\boxed{(\textbf{B})\ 2148}</imath>

~MrThinker

==Solution 3 (Counting Triplets by Line Length)==
We can solve this by grouping the straight lines based on how many points are actually on them. If a line has <imath>k</imath> points on it, the number of bad triplets we can pull from it is just <imath>\dbinom{k}{3}</imath>. 

First, the total number of ways to pick any 3 points out of the 25 coordinates is <imath>\dbinom{25}{3} = \frac{25 \cdot 24 \cdot 23}{3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1} = 2300</imath>. 

Now, we count the lines based on their point counts to find all the bad triplets:

* '''Lines with exactly 5 points:''' These are the full-length lines across the grid. We have <imath>5</imath> rows, <imath>5</imath> columns, and <imath>2</imath> long main diagonals. This gives <imath>5 + 5 + 2 = 12</imath> lines total. 
Triplets from this group: <imath>12 \times \dbinom{5}{3} = 12 \times 10 = 120</imath>.

* '''Lines with exactly 4 points:''' These are the diagonals directly next to the main ones. There are 2 sloping up and 2 sloping down, which gives <imath>4</imath> lines total. 
Triplets from this group: <imath>4 \times \dbinom{4}{3} = 4 \times 4 = 16</imath>.

* '''Lines with exactly 3 points:''' This group captures the remaining shorter lines and the hidden slopes:
# The tiny corner diagonals (<imath>2</imath> sloping up, <imath>2</imath> sloping down) <imath>\rightarrow</imath> 4 lines.
# The "knight-move" lines with slopes of <imath>\pm 2</imath> and <imath>\pm \frac{1}{2}</imath>. For each of these 4 unique slopes, there are exactly 3 parallel lines that hit exactly 3 points within the grid boundaries <imath>\rightarrow</imath> <imath>4 \times 3 = 12</imath> lines.
This gives a total of <imath>4 + 12 = 16</imath> lines with exactly 3 points. 
Triplets from this group: <imath>16 \times \dbinom{3}{3} = 16 \times 1 = 16</imath>.

Adding up all the bad triplets gives: <imath>120 + 16 + 16 = 152</imath>.

Subtracting these from the total pool gives the number of triangles with positive area: <imath>2300 - 152 = \boxed{(\textbf{B})\ 2148}</imath>.

~viviviiccotrrr1098
